messages.body_plain:
I have a developmental series where cartilage is formed at different times. I would like to place landmarks on the cartilage at two different developmental stages and was wondering what the best way of doing this was when some structures don't exist in one developmental stage compared to the other?

I imagine that placing as many similar landmarks as possible between each dev.stage, then removing those extra landmarks when it comes down to analysing dev.stage differences would be an option....is there another way?

Thanks! :-)
Sam

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Is it possible to compare groups with different landmarks?
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Is it possible to compare groups with different landmarks?
messages.body_plain:
Sam,

For GM analyses one does require a common set of landmarks, as these are the anatomical ‘bits’ that derive correspondence across specimens. This is directly akin to what one does with other biological comprisons: compare length vs. length across groups, or genetic variation in CytB vs. CytB across groups. Makes little sense to try to compare groups using different subsets of variables.

With GM, when there are some non-corresponding landmarks, two options are possible. First, one may remove the landmarks present in group A but not in group B, so the remaining set of landmarks is common to both. Alternatively, one may attempt to estimate the positions of missing landmarks using imputation methods. Two such methods have been examined in the context of GM and both are in geomorph. Note that before using these I would strongly recommend reading the primary literature on the topic. One may find useful references in the help file for the function ‘estimate.missing.’

Dean

messages.subject: Calculating directional asymmetry value for object symmetry specimen
messages.subject_clean: Calculating directional asymmetry value for object symmetry specimen
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Question 1: If I have a set of specimens which are object symmetry, how could I calculate directional asymmetry (DA) score for this set of specimen? I noted that after using bilat.symm function in geomorph, DA.component
could be extracted, which contains two sets of coordinates. I guess DA score of the sample could be calculated from DA.component, can anyone show me the code necessary to derive DA score?

Question 2: A possibly related question is how (appreciated if R code is provided) to obtain the Procrustes distance between two specimens after GPA. I think I can calculate the Procrustes distance between the original and reflected and relabled mirrors for each specimen and averaging the Procrustes distance across all specimens to obtain DA score for my entire sample.

Question3: A third question which is unrelated to the previous two is that I noted that Procrustes Variance is used in Morphol.disparity function to compare morphological disparity across groups. Procrustes Variance is explained in the user manual as "the sum of the diagonal elements of the group covariance matrix." But where can I find some more detailed mathematical definition of Procrustes Variance?

Thank you very much for your help!

Best regards,
Patrick Wen

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] phylogenetically corrected PCA in geomorph
messages.body_plain:
Chris, both PCA with the phylogeny superimposed (so-called phylomorphospaces), and phylogenetic PCA (PPCA) have been used to view tangent space.  Presently, geomorph only allows for the former, though PPCA is on our list of future updates.

For a more thorough understanding of the differences between the two and what PPCA actually does, and does not do, I recommend a careful read of Polly et al. 2013 in Hystrix. It shows clearly what PPCA actually is and how it is related to PCA.

>From my perspective, PPCA is not strictly ‘necessary’ as a procedure. Unlike PGLS where non-independence must be accounted for during the statistical evaluation of regression or anova, PCA has no such issues (there is no hypotheses test in PCA containing an assumption of independence, and so accounting for it is not necessary).

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] phylogenetically corrected PCA in geomorph
messages.body_plain:
Dean kind of beat me to the point I wanted to make, but I’ll add more to his perspective.  The term, "phylogenetically corrected PCA” is a bit dangerous, in my opinion.  PCA is nothing more than finding the major axes of variation in a data space, given a covariance matrix.  The phylogenetic “correction” is less precise to me than recognizing that a phylogenetically-informed covariance matrix is what is used to obtain the principal components.  The difference between a standard PCA with phylogeny superimposed and a phylogenetic PCA is merely a shift in origin from the data centroid to the estimated phylogenetic mean, and rotation based on the phylogeny rather than just the data covariance.  The geometric relationships of all points in this space remain unchanged.  I suppose with phylogenetic PCA, the covariance matrix has been “corrected”, but the PCA itself, has not been changed in any way.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Patrick,

shape.predictor is like a mapping function to map how shape changes along some predictor vectors.  In your previous post you referenced plotTangentSpace.  A component of that function is to map shape change along PC axes.  Yes, one can get PCs and use shape.predctor to get the same deformation grids for maximum values along the first PC, for example, as one would get in plotTangentSpace.  What you proposed with just submitting the means to plotTangentSpace is different, as it would find different PCs, thus different predictors.

1. The previous code did indeed show how to project means onto different PCs.
2. They might not be different, unless there were other factors taken into account.  The preds$symJord is the predicted vector, given the model, which is the same as the mean but does not have to be if there is a different model.

It seems to me that you are struggling with multiple ways to do the same thing and questioning why one would do something they could do one way a different way?  Does a linear model not estimate means if all it contains are factors for constructing the means?  So, in this case there is no difference but to emphasize what the difference is, for example, add centroid size to the model and now shape.predictor is not estimating means but some kind of allometric projection.

Cheers
Mike

Is it possible to do this? How do I obtain R2 values, slopes and intercepts for the levels within my each of my factors?

Any help in this regard would be appreciated

Candice

The procD.lm provides Rsq values for each factor and coefficients as output.  You can also use advanced.procD.lm but the Rsq values might not mean what you want them to mean because if you compare models sequentially - e.g., A to A+B, A+B to A+B+C, etc - the total SS will change in each comparison.  The procD.lm ANOVA table has one total SS from which all effect Rsq are calculated.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Candice,

The simple answer to your question is a, “yes,” but it is not an ideal analytical solution, in my opinion.  This is accomplished by subsetting your data by groups and performing simple linear regression, group by group, to get the Rsq values.

Doing that takes one away from a model comparison approach.  The Homogeneity of Slopes test is a model comparison approach.  It compares a model with a common allometry to one with separate allometries (if your covariate is specimen size).  The Rsq for that test is the amount (fraction) of SS gained by the extra parameters required to model separate slopes.  If significant, then you can state, “The unique allometries model explained XX% more variation than a common allometry model, which was significant.”  But to then try to partition that into separate Rsq values does not make much sense because these would not be the amount of variation explained by each group's regression; it would be the amount explained by each group's regression given all other groups’ regressions.

If the latter is what you are determined to do - and we do not have that as an option, because again, it makes little sense to us - here is how you can do that.  First, record the total SS from a procD.lm ANOVA table.  Second, acquire both the model design (X) and the coefficients (B) from the procD.lm output.  Multiplying these gives the fitted values; i.e., Fitted = X %*% B.  Third, systematically zero out one of the rows of the B matrix to eliminate one slope; find new fitted values; i.e., Fitted.r1 <- X %*% B.r1, where the .r1 refers to removed coefficients for 1st group.  Fourth, find the trace of the difference in sums of squares and cross-products matrices; i.e., sum(diag(crossprod(Fitted) - crossprod(Fitted.r1))).  This is the SS of the difference between all slopes and all slopes except the one that was removed with 0s in B.  Thus, it tells you how “heavy” that slope was.  Fifth, divide this value by the total SS and now you have the Rsq for one group given the unique slopes of the other groups.  Do this for all groups, one by one.

Or, alternatively, use the pairwise slopes test available in advanced.procD.lm and compare the length(distances) among groups to find out which group has significantly more or less shape variation change per unit of size than the others.  This is a hypothesis test and more informative than qualitative comparison of Rsq values.  If qualitative comparison is okay, then my first suggestion is probably the most parsimonious action.

I hope that makes sense!

Cheers!
Mike

Sorry, Candice, I misunderstood your question.

geomorph works with landmark shape data. One possibility would be to do a subsampling of your outline data to produce semilandmarks, using the digit.curves() function of geomorph, and possibly complement these with some fixed landmarks, which could then be used in a landmark-based shape analysis. In that case, you would need to superimpose your data using gpagen() with the curves argument, and then do the PCA using plotTangentSpace. But this is an analytically completely different solution compared to outline analysis using EFA.

Alternatively, the PCA and scatter-plotting part of plotTangentSpace are both based on the prcomp() base function of R, so producing plots with your EFA-treated data should be straightforward by setting uniform plot() arguments in R.

Hope this helps,
Antigoni
